answer:
**Downsampling can destroy the evidence before the model sees it.** If a 2200-pixel-high page is reduced to 224 pixels, a character originally 20 pixels high becomes roughly two pixels high. A decimal point or minus sign may vanish entirely. More language-model reasoning cannot reliably reconstruct an erased distinction. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929)

Dynamic high-resolution encoding addresses this by supplying detailed tiles along with a global view. The thumbnail shows where columns and sections lie; tiles preserve small characters. Coordinates and overlap help reconnect text that crosses tile boundaries.

**Detail creates its own costs.** More tiles produce more visual tokens, memory use, and downstream attention work. Overlap can duplicate text; separate crops can obscure reading order or attach a value to a header in another tile. A system needs a reconstruction strategy, not just a pile of enlarged patches.

Evaluate by original text size, page density, and table complexity. Test numeric punctuation and superscripts explicitly. For a question about one row, targeted high-resolution crops may be more efficient than encoding the entire page at maximum detail. Preserve source coordinates so extracted answers can be checked against the image. Good natural-image classification performance does not establish reliable small-text document reading.

**Technical details and references.**

A full page compressed to 224×224 can reduce small characters to a few pixels or less; information lost in resampling cannot be recovered reliably by a language prior. Fixed-size patches further limit spatial granularity. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929)

Dynamic high-resolution systems encode several detailed tiles plus a global thumbnail. The thumbnail supplies layout context, while tiles preserve small text. Retain tile coordinates and overlap so the model can connect lines and cells across boundaries. More tiles increase visual tokens, memory, and language-model cost.

Evaluate text-size and page-density slices, not only natural-image benchmarks. Tiling can duplicate or split content and confuse reading order; explicit document reconstruction or targeted crops may outperform indiscriminate full-page tiling for dense tables.
